idiom_name: mixin module included into the host (or a proc used as the policy)
implementation_notes: Ruby's modules are the direct analogue of policy classes: one module per axis (Storage, Eviction, Serialization) with a documented set of methods, composed into the host with include (instance methods) or extend (policies bound to a single object), while Module#prepend can override a method without losing the original and ancestors exposes the resulting order. The include/prepend chain replaces inheritance-based policy composition, and because Ruby is duck-typed the contract is documentation plus tests. For a single-method axis a proc or lambda passed to the constructor (or a block, as the standard library does with sort_by and Enumerable) is lighter still.
code_sketch:
module LruEviction
  def pick(keys) = keys.first
end
module FifoEviction
  def pick(keys) = keys.last
end

class Cache
  include LruEviction                     # policy composed into the host
  def initialize(items = {}) = @items = items
end
Cache.new.extend(FifoEviction)            # per-object policy binding
pitfalls: Method-resolution order decides which mixin wins: two policies defining the same method silently shadow each other, so inspect ancestors when composing several modules.
include binds at class-body evaluation time: conditionally including a policy at run time does not update objects already created (and lazily loaded constants may not exist yet).
extend mutates an object's singleton class: memoized or cached instances keep the old policy, and per-object mixing complicates debugging and serialization.
